Name: ENUM-Overflow Promotion to Reference Product (6-value cap)
Requirement: A categorical `value_regex` pipe-enum has a HARD CAP of 6 values. If >6 candidate values, leave `value_regex` EMPTY and append `[ENUM-REF-CANDIDATE: a
Example: If an `order` can only be in a handful of states like pending, paid or shipped, you can list those values inline. But a `country` field with 190 possible values is too many to list, so it should become its own lookup table that orders point to.

Name: value_regex Empty for Non-STRING Columns
Requirement: `value_regex` MUST be EMPTY for DATE, TIMESTAMP, BOOLEAN, INT/INTEGER, BIGINT, SMALLINT, TINYINT, DECIMAL(...), DOUBLE, FLOAT — the type already constrains the value. Regex is ONLY valid on STRING columns needing a specific format (phone, email, postal, ISO code, SKU). Never `true\
Example: A list of allowed text values only makes sense for text fields like a phone number or postal code. You should not put one on a yes/no field or a whole-number count, because the column's type already controls what can go in it.

Name: Attribute Business Glossary Term Expands Abbreviations
Requirement: Every attribute carries a business-glossary term: the business-friendly name with abbreviations fully expanded (full term, then the abbreviation in parentheses), not the raw abbreviation.
Example: Spell out abbreviations in the friendly business name. A column called `cust_acct_bal` should read as 'Customer Account Balance', not stay as the cryptic short form.

Name: Attribute References Its Governing Standard
Requirement: Every attribute that aligns to a business standard, governing body, or regulatory source must record that reference (e.g. the financial, privacy, or security standard it conforms to).
Example: If a field follows an official rule, note which one. A `national_id` field should mention the national identity standard it follows, and a credit card number field should reference the payment card security standard.

Name: FK-Add Attribute Budget at Synthesis Ceiling
Requirement: During automatic FK synthesis (process-flow / cross-domain gates), no new FK column may be added to a source product already carrying ≥40 attributes (or ≥`max_attributes_per_product`); the FK add is skipped (budget full) so synthesized FKs never bloat a product past the attribute ceiling.
Example: When the system automatically adds a link from one table to another, it should not pile a new column onto a table that is already crammed full. If an `order` table already has 40 columns, skip adding more so it does not become bloated.

Name: Standard SQL Data Types
Requirement: Every column must use a standard SQL data type (STRING, BIGINT, INT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL(p,s), BOOLEAN, DATE, TIMESTAMP, or ARRAY/MAP/STRUCT). No language- or engine-specific type names.
Example: Use everyday standard column types. A `price` should be a decimal number, a `created_at` should be a timestamp, and a `customer_id` should be a whole number, not some unusual custom type.

Name: No Complex Types
Requirement: Do NOT use ARRAY, STRUCT, or MAP types.
Example: Avoid stuffing a list inside one column. Instead of cramming multiple tags into a single `tags` cell on a `product`, keep a separate table that links products to their tags.

Name: Boolean Format
Requirement: Boolean representation follows widget configuration: Boolean (True/False), Int (0/1), or String (Y/N).
Example: Pick one way to record yes/no answers and follow the chosen setting. If the choice is Y/N, then an `is_active` field on a `customer` holds 'Y' or 'N' rather than true/false.

Name: Consistent Booleans
Requirement: Boolean representation must be consistent across the model. Choose one format and apply everywhere.
Example: Record yes/no the same way everywhere. If a `customer` table uses true/false for active status, then an `order` table should not switch to 1/0 or Y/N for its own flags.

Name: Infer Types by Name
Requirement: When no type is specified, infer from attribute name pattern.
Example: When the type is not stated, guess it from the name. A field ending in `_date` is a date, one ending in `_amount` is a money value, and one starting with `is_` is a yes/no flag.

Name: Categorical Values via Regex
Requirement: Categorical attributes must define allowed values using pipe-separated format in value_regex.
Example: For a field with a fixed set of choices, list them. An `order_status` should spell out its allowed values like pending, confirmed, shipped, delivered and cancelled.

Name: value_regex Only on STRING Columns
Requirement: A value_regex constraint is valid only on STRING columns that need a specific format (phone, email, postal code, ISO code, SKU). For DATE, TIMESTAMP, BOOLEAN, INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL, DOUBLE and other typed columns the type already constrains the value, so value_regex must be empty.
Example: A format rule belongs only on text fields that need a shape, like a phone number or postal code. A yes/no `is_active` field or a numeric `order_count` should have no such rule because their type already limits them.

Name: Categorical Enum Capped at Six Values
Requirement: A categorical pipe-enum in value_regex holds at most six allowed values. A categorical attribute with more than six distinct values must instead be modelled as a reference/lookup entity linked by FK, rather than an inline enum.
Example: A short fixed list of choices can sit right in the column. An `order_status` with five values is fine inline, but a `country` with 190 values should become its own reference table that other tables point to.

Name: Table Classifications
Requirement: Every table must be classified: master_data, reference_data, transactional_data, or association_data.
Example: Label every table by what it holds. A `customer` is master data, a `country` is reference data, an `order` is transactional data, and an `enrollment` linking students to courses is association data.

Name: FK Type Compatibility
Requirement: FK source and target column data types must be compatible. Numeric FK must reference numeric PK. String FK must reference string PK. Cross-type references (STRING FK to BIGINT PK) are invalid.
Example: A link between tables must match types on both ends. A numeric `customer_id` in `order` can point to the numeric `customer_id` in `customer`, but a text field cannot point to a numeric one.

Name: Real Business Functions Only
Requirement: Domain names must represent real business functions. Generic catch-all names are forbidden.
Example: Name a business area after the real function it serves. Use a concrete name like 'fieldservice' or 'powergeneration' instead of a vague catch-all like 'services' or 'utilities'.

Name: Division Balance Rule
Requirement: Operations + Business divisions must comprise >=80% of all domains. Corporate division capped at <=20%.
Example: Most business areas should be customer-facing or operational, with only a small slice for internal back-office. In a 10-area model, at least eight should be operations or business and at most two should be corporate functions like HR.

Name: No Early Corporate
Requirement: Cannot add Corporate division domains until Operations has >=2 domains AND Business has >=2 domains.
Example: Build out the core business areas before adding internal ones. Have at least two operations areas and two business areas (like production, logistics, customer, sales) before adding finance or HR.

Name: Interleaved Filling
Requirement: Alternate Operations and Business domains when filling the model to maintain balance.
Example: When filling out the model, alternate between operational and customer-facing areas to keep them balanced, rather than stacking all of one kind first.

Name: Forbidden Domain Types
Requirement: analytics, reporting, insights, intelligence, bi, datawarehouse, data, system, integration, api, etl, logging are forbidden. This includes analytics-specific names: analytics, reporting, intelligence, insights, metrics, kpi, dashboard, bi, datawarehouse — these belong in the Gold layer, not the Silver data model.
Example: Reporting and analytics areas do not belong in the operational model. Names like 'analytics', 'reporting', 'dashboard' or 'datawarehouse' describe downstream reporting, not real business functions.

Name: Forbidden Generic Names
Requirement: Forbidden: utilities, infrastructure, services, support, platform, shared (reserved), common, core, base, general, misc, other, admin, auxiliary.
Example: Avoid vague filler names for a business area. 'admin', 'misc', 'common' or 'services' say nothing; use a clear name like 'hr' or 'finance' instead.

Name: No Domain Fragmentation
Requirement: Domain pairs with 30%+ overlapping products must be merged. Forbidden pairs: network+assurance, customer+client, billing+revenue.
Example: If two areas mostly overlap, merge them. A 'customer' area and a 'client' area covering the same people should become one, and 'billing' and 'revenue' should be combined.

Name: Org Chart Test
Requirement: For every domain: 'Would I find a department named this at the company headquarters?' If NO -> rename. Test: 'Would a recruiter post jobs in the [domain_name] department?'
Example: Ask whether a real company would have a department by that name. 'customer service' would pass because companies have that department, but a vague label like 'party' usually would not.

Name: Domain Fit Default KEEP
Requirement: DEFAULT for every product is KEEP in its current domain. Relocate only on OBVIOUS misplacement with >95% confidence.
Example: By default, leave each table in the area where it was placed. Only move a table to a different area when it is very clearly in the wrong place.

Name: Cross-Division Relocation Forbidden
Requirement: A product can ONLY be relocated within the SAME division. Cross-division relocation is ABSOLUTELY FORBIDDEN.
Example: A table can move within the same broad grouping but not jump across very different ones. An `employee` table in the HR group should not be relocated into the production group.

Name: Eponymous Entity Rule
Requirement: Entities named after their domain must NEVER be moved between domains.
Example: A table named after its own area should never leave that area. An `invoice` table living in the 'billing' area cannot be moved into 'finance'.

Name: Child Follows Parent
Requirement: Child tables must stay with their parent table's domain.
Example: Keep child tables with their parent. If `order` sits in the sales area, then `order_line_item` must stay in the sales area too.

Name: Domain Hard Ceiling
Requirement: Domain count hard ceiling = max_domains x 1.5. Exceeding this is a hard rejection.
Example: There is a firm upper limit on how many business areas a model can have. If the target is 18 areas, anything beyond 27 is rejected and the model is rebuilt.

Name: Merge High-Overlap Domains
Requirement: If two proposed domains would share 30%+ of the same tables, they should be merged.
Example: When two proposed areas would share most of their tables, combine them. If 'customer' and 'subscriber' both contain account, profile and contact, they describe the same thing and should merge.

Name: No Shared Domain Initially
Requirement: Do not create a 'shared' domain during initial model design. Let the consolidation phase handle it.
Example: Do not create a generic 'shared' area up front. Place something like a `party` table in 'customer' first, and let a later cleanup step pull truly shared tables together.

Name: Merge Small Domains
Requirement: Domains with fewer tables than the configured minimum may be merged into a related domain.
Example: A tiny area can be folded into a related one. A 'warranty' area with just two tables can merge into 'service', unless the user specifically asked to keep 'warranty'.

Name: Domain Bloat Ceiling (No Domain Owns >25% of Products)
Requirement: No single domain may own strictly more than 25% of all products in the model. A domain holding a disproportionate share signals an under-decomposed catch-all that should be split into focused business functions. The check is a post-mutation invariant: when any domain exceeds the fraction ceiling it fires [H1-BLOAT FIRED] and surfaces the offending domain, its product share, and rule id DOM-RUL-034 for corrective decomposition. USER VIBES ARE SUPREME: if the user explicitly pins a domain to hold most products, the directive wins (the guard is advisory SHOULD_FIX).
Example: No single area should own most of the tables. If one area called 'core' holds 12 of 20 tables while the rest are nearly empty, that area is doing too much and should be split into focused functions.

Name: Per-Division Target Ratios
Requirement: Domains SHOULD distribute across divisions per `divisions_ratios` ({operations:0.50, business:0.35, corporate:0.15}); the division taxonomy itself is industry-overridable (`divisions_taxonomy`, e.g. banking front/middle/back office). Per-division percentage targets, beyond the binary Ops+Bus≥80% / Corp≤20% rule.
Example: Spread business areas across operational, customer-facing and back-office groups in roughly set proportions, and adapt the grouping names to the industry (for a bank, front, middle and back office).

Name: Tier-2 Industry-Dependent Domain Names Allowed
Requirement: Forbidden domain names split into two tiers. Tier-1 (analytics, reporting, data, system, etl, logging, common, core, shared, platform…) are hard-blocked in ALL industries. Tier-2 (utilities, services, operations, support, regulatory, audit, technology, infrastructure, admin) are forbidden as vague EXCEPT when they are the canonical org-chart name in `business_context.data_domains` for THIS business. The blacklist MUST consult industry context, not reject unconditionally.
Example: Some area names are always banned, like 'analytics' or 'system'. Others like 'support' or 'regulatory' are only allowed when they are the genuine, recognized name for that function in this particular industry.

Name: Industry Vocabulary Must-Use / Prohibited Terms
Requirement: `industry_vocabulary = {must_use_terms, prohibited_terms}` defines terminology the model MUST use and generic terms it MUST avoid for the specific industry. Domain/product/attribute naming must honor must_use_terms and reject prohibited_terms, beyond the global forbidden-name blacklists.
Example: Each industry has preferred words to use and generic words to avoid. Name areas, tables and columns using the industry's real vocabulary and steer clear of the terms it considers too generic.

Name: Domain Description Conciseness Ceiling
Requirement: Domain descriptions MUST be concise: maximum 2-3 sentences (~100 chars for standards descriptions), focused on WHAT the domain owns, not exhaustive lists. Upper bound complementing the 20-char minimum and >70% overlap rules.
Example: Keep an area's description short. Two or three sentences saying what the area owns is enough; do not write a long exhaustive list.

Name: Subdomain Cross-Domain Name-Collision Qualified Rename
Requirement: No subdomain name may appear in more than one domain. When the same subdomain name occurs across domains it MUST be renamed to a domain-qualified form (shop_floor_order_execution vs procurement_order_execution) so subdomain names are globally unambiguous.
Example: A sub-area name should be unique across the whole model. If two areas both have an 'order execution' sub-area, rename each so it is clear which area it belongs to.

Name: Identical-Domain Detection Before Cross-Domain Linking
Requirement: Before creating cross-domain links, detect domain PAIRS that are actually the same domain (5+ products with same/similar names, products answering the same questions, >70% functional overlap), flag in `identical_domain_pairs` with a recommended primary, and recommend MERGE before linking rather than meshing two fragments.
Example: Before linking two areas together, check whether they are actually the same area in disguise. If they share most of their tables, merge them first instead of stitching two halves together.

Name: MVM Domains Tell a Complete WHO/WHAT/HOW Story
Requirement: A limited MVM domain set MUST collectively answer WHO the business serves (primary party domain, industry-natural term), WHAT it offers (product/service), HOW transactions flow (transactional), plus any essential operational domain. Obscure/edge-case domains that don't contribute to the core narrative are avoided.
Example: A small, focused model should still tell a complete story: who the business serves, what it offers, and how transactions flow. Leave out obscure side topics that do not contribute to that core story.

Name: Division Classification — Exactly One, Decision-Tested
Requirement: Each domain gets EXACTLY ONE division with no overlap, decided by explicit tests: "directly touches customers?"→business vs "enables service delivery?"→operations; "generates revenue?"→business vs "supports those who do?"→corporate; "could the business survive a week without this domain's data?"→corporate.
Example: Put each business area in exactly one group, decided by simple questions: does it touch customers directly, does it bring in revenue, or could the business run for a week without it.

Name: Distribute Shared Tables
Requirement: Tables in 'shared' domain should be moved to their natural owner, unless cross-cutting reference data used by 3+ domains.
Example: Move tables out of a generic 'shared' bucket to their natural home, unless they are reference data used by many areas. A `country` table used by five areas can stay shared; a `tariff` used only by billing should move to billing.

Name: FK Population Sequence Documented; Pre-Parent Children Get Nullable FK
Requirement: Every FK should document when it is populated relative to its target's creation (at creation, during a later process, or on completion). A child record that legitimately exists before its parent must carry a NULLABLE FK with a documented enrichment path, rather than having the relationship dropped.
Example: Note when a link gets filled in relative to the record it points to. A charge that exists before its invoice is created can carry an empty invoice link at first, filled in once the invoice is generated, rather than dropping the relationship.

Name: FK Target Must Exist
Requirement: FK must reference a product that exists in the model. Broken FK references are auto-resolved.
Example: A link must point to a table that actually exists in the model. An `order` linking to a `customer` only works if there really is a `customer` table.

Name: No Bidirectional FKs
Requirement: NEVER create FK relationships in BOTH directions between the same tables (A->B and B->A is forbidden).
Example: Two tables should not point at each other. If an `order` links to a `customer`, then the `customer` table must not also link back to that `order`.

Name: FK Column Must Exist
Requirement: FK attribute must exist in the source product before linking.
Example: The linking column has to exist before you can use it for a link. You cannot link `order` to `customer` through a `customer_id` column if `order` has no such column.

Name: FK Must Reference PK
Requirement: FK must reference the primary key of the target product.
Example: A link must point to the unique identifier of the target table. An `order` should link to `customer` through `customer_id`, not through the customer's email address.

Name: System ID Exemption
Requirement: External/system identifier columns are NOT FK columns. Patterns: *_reference, *_ref, *_code, *_number, *_hash, *_token.
Example: Reference numbers from outside systems are not real links. Columns like `external_reference`, `legacy_code` or `batch_number` are just identifiers and should not be treated as pointers to another table.

Name: Broken FK and Reference Resolution
Requirement: FKs referencing non-existent columns/products must be resolved: LINK, CREATE, DROP, or KEEP_AS_IS. Additionally, attributes that reference non-existent products must be removed from the model — if a domain or product was deleted, all FK references to it become orphaned and must be cleaned up.
Example: Links that point at something no longer in the model must be cleaned up. If a 'billing' area was deleted, any column still pointing to `billing.invoice` is now dangling and should be removed.

Name: Self-Referencing FK Rules
Requirement: Self-referencing FKs (source_product == target_product) are ONLY allowed with a contextually meaningful label prefix. The FK column name must NEVER be the same as the table PK. If you cannot articulate a clear business reason for the self-reference, do NOT create it.
Example: A table can point back to itself only when there is a clear reason and a descriptive column name. An `employee` table can have a `manager_employee_id` pointing to another employee, but it must not reuse the plain `employee_id` for that.

Name: Potential and Orphaned FK Detection
Requirement: Columns ending with PK suffix (_id, _key, _pk) are potential FK candidates unless exempted as system identifiers. Any such column without a foreign_key_to value is an orphaned FK candidate that should be linked to its target table if one exists.
Example: A column that looks like a link but is not connected to anything should be hooked up. If `order` has a `warehouse_id` with no target and a `warehouse` table exists, connect them.

Name: FK Column Rename
Requirement: FK columns that don't end with the target PK name must be renamed. 4 strategies available.
Example: Rename a linking column so it clearly ends with the target's identifier. A vague `store_ref` pointing to a `location` table should become `store_location_id`.

Name: Parent-Child FK Protected
Requirement: Parent-child FKs (child->parent direction) must NEVER be broken during cycle resolution. These are the structural backbone of the model. This protection applies during cycle resolution, model optimization, and any restructuring operation.
Example: The link from a child table up to its parent is essential and must never be cut. An `order_line` pointing to its `order` is the backbone of the model and stays even when other links are trimmed.

Name: Multiple FKs to Same Target — Labeling Required
Requirement: When a table has more than one FK pointing to the SAME target table, each FK column MUST have a distinct, contextually meaningful label prefix describing the business role. Two columns with the same name pointing to the same target is INVALID. Label prefixes must reflect actual business meaning — generic labels like fk1_, fk2_, ref_a_ are forbidden. During quality checks, multiple FK columns to the same target without distinct labels are flagged as anomalies.
Example: When one table points to the same target twice, each link needs a meaningful name. A `shipment` can have both `origin_warehouse_id` and `destination_warehouse_id` pointing to `warehouse`, but not two columns with the same name.

Name: Duplicate FK Detection and Removal
Requirement: If a table has two or more FK columns pointing to the same target table without a clear business reason, keep only one. Detection: two or more FK columns on the SAME table pointing to the SAME target table. Resolution: if no clear distinct business roles, keep only one. If distinct roles exist (billing vs shipping), keep both with proper label prefixes.
Example: Drop a duplicate link that serves no distinct purpose. Two columns both pointing to `customer` with no real difference should become one, but a `billing_address_id` and `shipping_address_id` both pointing to `address` are kept because they mean different things.

Name: Fully Qualified FKs
Requirement: FK reference values must use the fully qualified path format: domain.product.column.
Example: Write a link using its full address: area, table, then column. 'customer.profile.profile_id' is clear, while just 'profile_id' is ambiguous about where it lives.

Name: No Placeholder FKs
Requirement: FK reference values containing placeholder or garbage text are invalid and must be cleared.
Example: Placeholder or junk link values are not allowed. A link set to 'tbd', 'none' or 'unknown.table.column' is meaningless and must be cleared.

Name: Self-Ref FK Column Naming
Requirement: A self-referencing FK column MUST have a different name than the table's PK. The FK must use a contextual prefix describing the hierarchical relationship (e.g., manager_, parent_, reporting_). If the FK column name equals the PK name, the relationship is always invalid.
Example: A self-pointing link needs a name different from the table's own identifier. An `employee` table uses `manager_employee_id` to point to another employee, never the plain `employee_id`.

Name: FK Name Equals Target PK Verbatim (No Double-Suffix)
Requirement: A FK column name MUST EQUAL the target table's PK column name verbatim, byte-for-byte. The configured PK suffix is ALREADY part of the target PK — DO NOT append it again. The only exception is a business-role disambiguation prefix (multiple FKs to the same target with distinct roles, or a self-referencing parent FK); the suffix portion MUST still equal the target PK verbatim. (v0.8.5 M1-FIX, alias=fk-name-helper-field-widen)
Example: A linking column should match the target's identifier name exactly, without doubling the ending. If `customer` is identified by `customer_id`, the link in `order` is `customer_id`, never `customer_id_id`.

Name: FK Temporal Precedence
Requirement: A FK direction MUST follow the real-world chronological order of the business process. The SOURCE entity (holding the FK column) MUST come into existence AT THE SAME TIME OR LATER than the TARGET entity. An entity created EARLIER in the workflow CANNOT hold a FK to an entity created LATER. (v0.8.5 M3-FIX, alias=fk-temporal-precedence)
Example: A link must follow the real order of events. Since an invoice comes after an order, the invoice can point back to the order, but the order cannot point forward to an invoice that does not exist yet.

Name: FK Cardinality Correctness
Requirement: The FK column MUST live on the MANY side of a 1:N relationship. If entity X holds a single FK column pointing at entity Y but in the real world X relates to MANY Y's, the FK is on the WRONG side and must be reversed. For TRUE 1:1 relationships the FK lives on whichever side is created later. For M:N relationships, neither side holds a FK — introduce a junction table. (v0.8.5 M4-FIX, alias=fk-cardinality-correctness)
Example: The link lives on the 'many' side. Since one customer has many orders, the `customer_id` link sits on `order`, not an `order_id` link on `customer`.

Name: Junction Table Purity
Requirement: A junction / associative / membership / link / cross-reference entity that exists to model M:N between exactly two other entities A and B MUST hold EXACTLY (i) a FK to A, (ii) a FK to B, and OPTIONALLY (iii) relationship-attribute columns describing properties of the link itself (effective-from, effective-until, role-in-relationship, weight, rank). It MUST NOT carry a FK to any third entity C outside {A, B}. If a junction has FKs to three or more unrelated entities, it is no longer a junction — it is a hidden TRANSACTION_HEADER and the third FK is invalid. (v0.8.5, alias=junction-purity)
Example: A pure connector table that links two things should hold only those two links plus details about the connection. An `enrollment` joining students and courses can carry a grade or date, but should not also point to an unrelated payment.

Name: FK-Addition Attribute Budget + Canonical-Code Advisory
Requirement: FK-link proposals MUST respect a per-product attribute budget: when a source product already has >= max_attributes_per_product attributes, new FK additions to it are skipped so the product does not blow past its sizing ceiling (DROP/KEEP are never budget-blocked; CREATE evaluates the budget against the new parent). Separately, when a product carries more than 10 unlinked string columns bearing canonical FK suffixes (_code/_number/_key/_ref/_name/_type/_status/_flag/_abbr), an advisory note is emitted for the FK linker. max_attrs<=0 disables the budget (backward-compatible). Emits [REL-RUL-035 FIRED].
Example: Do not add a new link to a table that is already at its column limit, and flag tables with many unconnected code-like columns for review. A table three columns under its limit links normally; one already over the limit is skipped.

Name: Business-Process FK Path Completeness
Requirement: For every end-to-end business process the model claims to support (e.g. order-to-cash, procure-to-pay), the chain of entities in that process must be connected end-to-end by foreign keys, directly or through documented intermediate entities. A required link in a declared process flow must not be missing.
Example: Every business flow the model claims to support must be connected end to end. For order-to-cash, you should be able to trace quote to order to invoice to payment through links; a missing step means the flow is broken.

Name: Cross-Domain FK Must Be Semantically Valid
Requirement: Every cross-domain FK must connect two entities whose business meanings genuinely relate. A FK created only because two unrelated tables happen to share a column name (both have segment_id) is invalid and must be removed. Structural validity (target exists, types match, no cycle) is necessary but NOT sufficient — business meaning must also hold.
Example: A link between areas must make real business sense, not just share a column name. If a marketing table and a network table both have `segment_id` but mean different things, do not link them.

Name: Person/Role FK Targets a Person Entity
Requirement: A FK column whose name denotes a person role (*_inspector_id, *_auditor_id, *_reviewer_id, *_approver_id, *_technician_id, *_officer_id, *_buyer_id, etc.) must reference a person/party entity (e.g. employee, actor), never a non-person table. If no person entity exists, one must be created to hold the reference.
Example: A column naming a person's role must point to a people table. A `work_order.inspector_id` should link to an `employee` table, not to an equipment table.

Name: FK Namespace Coherence
Requirement: For every FK, the domain named in the foreign_key_to target path must match the domain named in that FK's description. A description that says 'links to asset.equipment' while foreign_key_to points at workforce.equipment is incoherent and must be corrected.
Example: A link's description must name the same area it actually points to. If the description says it points to the asset area's equipment, the link itself must point to `asset.equipment`, not somewhere else.

Name: Metric-View Columns Must Resolve to Real Attributes
Requirement: Every column referenced by a metric view (each dimension, measure, and filter) must resolve to an attribute that actually exists on the referenced product. A metric view referencing a column that no longer exists after normalization or rename is invalid and must be repaired or dropped.
Example: Every column used in a report definition must really exist on the table it claims to use. A report measuring the total of `net_amount` on `order` is broken if `order` has no `net_amount` column.

Name: No Product Prefix on Attributes
Requirement: Column names MUST NOT repeat the table name as a prefix, except for the primary key.
Example: Do not repeat the table name in its own columns, except for the identifier. In an `account` table, use `balance` and `type`, not `account_balance` and `account_type`; only `account_id` keeps the prefix.

Name: PK Naming Pattern
Requirement: Primary key names follow the pattern: table_name + suffix (default: _id).
Example: The identifier column is named after its table. A `customer` table has `customer_id`, an `order` table has `order_id`.

Name: FK Column Suffix Rule
Requirement: Foreign key column names must END WITH the target table's primary key name. Descriptive prefixes are allowed.
Example: A linking column ends with the identifier name of the table it points to. A `billing_address_id` ends in `address_id` so it clearly links to the `address` table.

Name: Column Name Max Length
Requirement: Column names must not exceed 50 characters.
Example: Keep column names reasonably short. A clear name like `monthly_transaction_amount` is fine, but a 65-character mouthful should be trimmed down.

Name: Semantic Attribute Names
Requirement: Column names must be clear, semantic, and human-readable. Prioritize clarity over brevity.
Example: Use clear, readable column names over cryptic shorthand. Prefer `mean_time_between_failures` to 'mtbf' so anyone can understand it.

Name: Preserve Unit Qualifiers
Requirement: Preserve important qualifiers in column names: units (kg, mwh, percent), rates (per_min, per_hour), and standard terms.
Example: Keep important qualifiers like units and rates in the name. Use `energy_consumption_mwh` rather than just `energy_consumption` so the unit is not lost.

Name: Unique Attribute Names
Requirement: Each attribute name must be unique within the product. No two columns within the same table may have the same name. Duplicates are auto-deduplicated.
Example: Two columns in the same table cannot share a name. If an `order` table needs two status fields, name them `fulfillment_status` and `payment_status`, not both `status`.

Name: Bare Attribute Name Prohibition
Requirement: Generic attribute names (status, type, name, description, date, code, category, level, priority, amount, quantity, rate, score, value, count) MUST be prefixed with business context from their parent product. A bare generic name is always a violation.
Example: Generic words need their table's context as a prefix. In an `order` table, a status field should be `order_status`, and in a `facility` table the name field should be `facility_name`.

Name: PK Casing Boundary Preservation
Requirement: The PK composition pipeline MUST preserve PascalCase/camelCase word boundaries through naming convention round-trips. sanitize_name() lowercases input which destroys boundaries; the helper MUST pre-encode PascalCase word boundaries as underscores BEFORE sanitization so word boundaries survive. (v0.8.5 M2-FIX, alias=pk-casing-preserve-boundaries)
Example: When converting names between styles, keep word breaks intact. An entity called 'CatalogItem' should produce `CatalogItemId`, not collapse into a single garbled word.

Name: Bare Reserved-Word Attribute Prefixing
Requirement: An attribute whose name is a bare generic SQL/structural reserved word (status, type, name, code, date, key, value, ...) MUST be prefixed with its owning product name -> {product}_{bare_name} so the column is self-describing and join-safe. EXEMPT: primary keys, foreign keys, already-prefixed names, audit sentinels, and any name the user explicitly directs to keep/preserve (USER-KING). Bounded to 50 text-field edits per diff. Emits [BARE_ATTR_PREFIX FIRED].
Example: A column with a bare generic name gets its table name added in front. A plain `status` in an `order` table becomes `order_status`, but identifiers and anything the user asked to keep are left alone.

Name: Single-Word Domains
Requirement: Domain names must be exactly one word, lowercase, SQL-compliant, no underscores, and no longer than 20 characters.
Example: A business area name is a single lowercase word with no underscores and not too long. 'customer', 'sales' and 'logistics' are fine, but 'customer_service' (two words) is not.

Name: Singular Domain Names
Requirement: Domain names must be singular, never plural. Exception: naturally singular terms ending in 's' like logistics, sales, or operations.
Example: Use the singular form for area names. Use 'customer' not 'customers', and 'product' not 'products', though naturally singular words like 'logistics' and 'sales' are fine.

Name: Snake Case Default
Requirement: All names (domains, tables, columns) must use snake_case by default. All names are generated in snake_case first, then converted to the user-selected casing convention (PascalCase, camelCase, SCREAMING_CASE).
Example: Build all names in lowercase-with-underscores first, then convert to whatever style the user chose. `customer_order_date` is correct; a hyphenated 'customer-order-date' is not.

Name: Valid Identifier Characters
Requirement: All names must be lowercase, contain only letters, numbers, and underscores, and must not start with a digit.
Example: Names use only lowercase letters, numbers and underscores, and cannot start with a number. `order_date` and `address_line_1` are valid; 'Order_Date' and '3rd_party_id' are not.

Name: Industry Jargon Usage
Requirement: Use industry jargon only when universally recognized. Otherwise prefer the full term.
Example: Only use industry shorthand when it is widely understood. In telecom, well-known terms are fine, but inventing cryptic shortenings like 'cust_nm' for customer name is not.

Name: Digit-Start Names
Requirement: Names starting with a digit get an underscore prefix automatically.
Example: A name that would start with a digit gets an underscore added in front, so '3pl' becomes '_3pl'.

Name: Product Name Length
Requirement: Table names must be 1 to 3 words, lowercase, and no longer than 30 characters.
Example: A table name is one to three words, lowercase, and not too long. 'profile', 'rate_schedule' and 'order_line_item' are fine; a long phrase like 'monthly_aggregated_customer_transaction_summary' is too much.

Name: No Domain Prefix on Products
Requirement: Table names MUST NOT repeat the domain name as a prefix. In domain 'customer', the table should be 'account', NOT 'customer_account'.
Example: Do not repeat the area name in its tables. In the 'customer' area, name the table `account`, not `customer_account`, since the full address already shows the area.

Name: Association Table Naming
Requirement: Association (junction) table names must NOT repeat the domain name as a prefix. Use semantically meaningful names. Names must be semantically meaningful business terms. Generic-only names (link, mapping, junction, bridge, xref) are forbidden. If the only name you can think of is 'link' or 'mapping', the M:N relationship probably should not exist.
Example: A connector table gets a real business name, not a generic one. A table joining students and courses should be called `enrollment`, never 'link', 'mapping' or 'junction'.

Name: Merged Table Naming
Requirement: When two duplicate tables are merged into a shared location, use the most generic, domain-agnostic name.
Example: When merging two duplicate tables, give the result a neutral, generic name. Merging a customer profile and a partner contact should produce something like `party`, not a name that favours one side.

Name: Forbidden Product Suffixes
Requirement: Products must NOT end with: _analysis, _analytics, _report, _summary, _aggregate, _dashboard, _metrics, _kpi, _score, _model, _prediction.
Example: Tables must not end with analytics-style suffixes. Names ending in `_report`, `_summary`, `_metrics` or `_prediction`, like 'revenue_analysis', do not belong in the operational model.

Name: Max Underscore Segments
Requirement: Product names may contain at most 3 underscore-separated segments (max 4 words).
Example: A table name has at most three underscore-separated parts. 'order_line_item' is fine, but 'monthly_aggregated_transaction_summary' has too many parts and should be simplified.

Name: Keep Names on Relocation
Requirement: When a table is moved to a different domain, keep its original name. Do not rename tables during relocation.
Example: When a table moves to a new area, it keeps its name. Moving `incident` from one area to another leaves it called `incident`; only its location changes.

Name: Conditional Domain Prefix
Requirement: A domain prefix in a product name is justified ONLY when another domain already has a table with the same base name, requiring disambiguation.
Example: Only prefix a table with its area name to avoid a name clash. If both sales and procurement need an order table, 'sales_order' and 'purchase_order' are justified; otherwise just call it `order`.

Name: Logical/Physical Name Match
Requirement: The physical table name must exactly match the product (logical) name in snake_case. No divergence between logical and physical names.
Example: The stored table name must match the logical name exactly. A table called `rate_schedule` is stored as `rate_schedule`, not 'tbl_rate_schedule' or 'RATE_SCHEDULE'.

Name: Denormalized Attribute Detection
Requirement: An attribute is denormalized only when it stores data belonging to a DIFFERENT entity accessible via FK join. >95% confidence required.
Example: A column is misplaced only if it really describes a different table you can already reach by a link. A `customer_name` on `order` is misplaced if `order` already links to `customer`.

Name: Self-Attribute Exemption
Requirement: If a table's own attribute has a prefix matching the table's own name, it is NOT denormalized.
Example: A column that describes its own table is fine. `customer_name` on the `customer` table is correct because it describes the customer itself.

Name: Measurement Exemption
Requirement: Physical measurements, quantities, or properties (depth, weight, volume) owned by the entity are NEVER denormalized.
Example: Physical measurements that belong to the thing itself are fine to keep. A `warehouse` legitimately owns its own latitude and longitude.

Name: Coordinates Exemption
Requirement: Physical entities (warehouse, facility, store, site, address) legitimately own their own lat/long coordinates.
Example: A physical place owns its own coordinates. A `store` keeping its latitude and longitude is correct because the store really is at that spot.

Name: Point-in-Time Snapshot Exemption
Requirement: Transactional/event records that snapshot data at time of event for audit/compliance purposes are NOT denormalized.
Example: A record that captures a value as it was at the moment of an event is fine to keep. An invoice storing the customer's address at billing time is a legitimate point-in-time record for audit purposes.

Name: Audit Trail Exemption
Requirement: Audit trail records MUST snapshot user information. Treating this as denormalized is a false positive.
Example: An audit log should keep a copy of the user's details at the time. Recording the user's name on the log is correct, because that person's record could change later.

Name: Exact Match Only
Requirement: Only flag denormalization when the prefix EXACTLY matches a table name. No synonym guessing.
Example: Only flag a column as misplaced when its prefix exactly matches a real table name. A `billing_amount` on `order` is only questioned if a table literally called `billing` exists.

Name: Conservative Bias
Requirement: When in doubt, DO NOT remove an attribute. False removals destroy data. Only flag with >95% confidence.
Example: When unsure, keep the column. Removing data by mistake is worse than leaving an extra column, so only remove when you are nearly certain.

Name: No Calculated Metrics
Requirement: Do NOT include pre-calculated KPIs, aggregates, or metrics. These are derived in the Gold layer.
Example: Do not store pre-calculated totals or scores; those belong in reporting. Drop things like a customer's total lifetime value or an account's average monthly balance.

Name: No Speculative Columns
Requirement: Only include attributes for CURRENTLY implemented capabilities. No futuristic/emerging tech columns.
Example: Only include columns for things the business actually does today. Drop speculative fields like a 'blockchain_hash' or 'ai_prediction_score' that serve no current purpose.

Name: 3NF Enforcement
Requirement: Full Third Normal Form: no partial dependencies and no transitive dependencies.
Example: Each column should describe its own table directly. An `order` should not store `customer_name` when it already links to `customer`, since that detail belongs on the customer.

Name: No Self-PK Declared as Orphaned FK
Requirement: An attribute whose name-prefix equals its owning product name AND which is declared as that product's primary key MUST NOT also carry a foreign_key_to pointing back to its own domain.product. This catches normalization mis-wiring a self-PK as a self-referencing FK (which would create a spurious cycle). Conservative True when the product/domain is missing.
Example: A table's own identifier must not also be set up as a link pointing back to itself. A `customer` table's `customer_id` should be just the identifier, not also a self-link, which would create a confusing loop.

Name: 3NF Transitive Dependencies Extracted to Lookups
Requirement: When a non-key column depends on another non-key column (a transitive dependency), the dependent columns must be extracted into a new lookup entity keyed by their determinant, and the source product references that lookup via FK, rather than carrying the transitively-dependent columns inline.
Example: When one detail depends on another, split it into a lookup. If `order` carries zip code plus the city and state that depend on it, move city and state into a postal-code lookup and keep zip code as the link.

Name: FK Addition Surrenders Now-Redundant Columns
Requirement: When a FK to a target entity is added to a product, any column on that product that merely duplicates a column retrievable from the target via the new FK must be removed. Only columns visible on the source AND present on the target are removed; thin reference tables (id/name/code only) only surrender <entity>_name / <entity>_code.
Example: Once you add a link to another table, drop columns you can now get through that link. After adding a `supplier_id` link to a line item, the `supplier_name` copied onto it can be removed.

Name: No Denormalized Natural Key Beside Its FK
Requirement: When a product has both a FK to an entity (<entity>_id) AND a natural-key column for the same entity (suffix _number/_code/_name/_reference/_no/_num/_ref/_identifier/_label/_sku/_barcode/_serial), the natural key is reachable through the FK and must be dropped, unless it has its own outbound FK or is user-protected.
Example: Do not keep a second identifier for something you already link to. If `order` links to a supplier by `supplier_id`, a separate `supplier_code` is redundant and should be dropped.

Name: FK-Triggered Redundant-Column Consolidation
Requirement: When a FK source->target link is established, source columns that duplicate target columns (source column = target_base + a suffix that exists as an attribute on the target) must be removed and any references repointed, so duplicated data is consolidated behind the FK.
Example: After linking two tables, remove copied-over columns that duplicate the target. Once a `shipment` links to a `warehouse`, a `warehouse_city` copied onto the shipment is removed.

Name: Point-in-Time Override Values Kept on Event Tables
Requirement: On transactional / event / audit tables, a value that captures an execution-specific override at the moment of the event must be kept even after a FK to the defining entity is added — it is a point-in-time snapshot, not denormalization. Denormalization is only flagged on master/reference entities.
Example: On event records, keep a value that captured what actually happened at the time. An order line should keep the `unit_price_at_sale` even though the product has a current list price, because it records the price actually charged.

Name: Self-PK Must Not Be Declared as a Self-FK
Requirement: A product's own primary-key column must not also carry a foreign_key_to pointing back at its own domain.product.pk. Wiring a self-PK as a self-referencing FK creates a spurious cycle and is invalid.
Example: A table's identifier must not double as a link to itself. A `customer_id` should not point back to its own customer table; a hierarchy needs a separate `parent_customer_id` column.

Name: Domain-Level FK Resolution
Requirement: FK columns often use DOMAIN NAMES as prefixes. Must resolve to domain's primary entity.
Example: A linking column often borrows an area name and must resolve to that area's main table. A `store_id` may resolve to the `store` table inside the 'location' area.

Name: Every Product Has PK
Requirement: Every product must have exactly one primary key attribute. Auto-inserted if missing.
Example: Every table needs exactly one identifier column. If a table is built without one, an identifier like `customer_id` is added automatically.

Name: PK Naming Convention
Requirement: PK column = {product_name}_{suffix} (default suffix: _id).
Example: The identifier column is the table name plus a standard ending. A `customer` table gets `customer_id`, an `order_line_item` table gets `order_line_item_id`.

Name: PK Data Type
Requirement: Primary keys MUST use the configured table_id_type (default: BIGINT).
Example: Identifier columns use the standard whole-number type. If one was set to text by mistake, it is corrected back to the standard numeric type.

Name: PK First Attribute
Requirement: PK must be the first attribute listed in the product's attribute list.
Example: The identifier is listed first in the table. The column order starts with `customer_id`, then first name, last name, email and so on.

Name: PK Exempt from Prefix Strip
Requirement: PK attributes (e.g., customer_id) are EXEMPT from the 'no product prefix' naming rule.
Example: The identifier keeps its table-name prefix even though other columns drop theirs. `customer_id` stays as is so it can be recognized when other tables link to it.

Name: Association PK Naming
Requirement: Association product PK = {association_name}_{primary_key_suffix}.
Example: A connector table's identifier is named after the connector itself. A table joining students and courses gets `enrollment_id`, not a mash-up of the two table names.

Name: PK Not in Orphaned FK List
Requirement: A table's own PK must NEVER be included in the orphaned FK list during normalization checks.
Example: A table's own identifier is never treated as a broken link. `customer_id` on the `customer` table is the identifier, not a dangling pointer.

Name: PK Detection Patterns
Requirement: PK detection: ends with _id, _key, _code, _num, or equals 'id'. Name constructed by stripping domain prefix.
Example: Columns ending in standard identifier endings are recognized as identifiers. `order_id`, `customer_key` and `product_code` are all treated as potential identifiers.

Name: Junction Table PKs
Requirement: Association (junction) tables follow the same PK naming: association_table_name + _id.
Example: Connector tables follow the same identifier rule. An `enrollment` gets `enrollment_id` and an `assignment` gets `assignment_id`, not a combination of the joined tables.

Name: Validate PK Names
Requirement: A PK name is invalid if: empty, bare suffix alone, starts with underscore, equals 'id', or does not end with suffix.
Example: An identifier name must be complete and well-formed. For `customer`, `customer_id` is valid, while just 'id', '_id' or 'customer_code' are not valid identifiers.

Name: Strict Column Ordering
Requirement: Columns must follow strict ordering: PK, FKs, business attributes, housekeeping, history-tracking. Housekeeping columns (is_deleted, is_active, created_by, updated_by) come after business attributes. History-tracking columns (effective_from, effective_to, is_current, version_number) come last, after housekeeping.
Example: Order the columns consistently: identifier first, then links, then business details, then housekeeping like `created_by`, then history fields like `effective_from`. So an `order` lists `order_id`, `customer_id`, the order details, then the housekeeping and history columns.

Name: Junction Table Audit Columns
Requirement: Association tables with only FK columns must include minimum audit columns: created_at and created_by.
Example: A connector table with only links should still record who created it and when. An `enrollment` joining a student and a course should also carry `created_at` and `created_by`.

Name: Resolve Semantic Synonyms
Requirement: Attribute semantic synonyms must be resolved to one canonical name per table.
Example: If two columns mean the same thing, keep just one. A table with both `end_date` and `expiry_date` for the same concept should drop one of them.

Name: Canonical Attribute Categories — Hard Minimums by Entity Role
Requirement: Every product MUST be classified into ONE of the entity roles {MASTER_PARTY, MASTER_AGREEMENT, MASTER_RESOURCE, TRANSACTION_HEADER, TRANSACTION_LINE, JUNCTION, EVENT_LOG, REFERENCE_LOOKUP, OTHER} and the role's minimum semantic-category set MUST be present beyond the PK. Categories are abstract (e.g. IDENTITY_LABEL, LIFECYCLE_STATUS, BUSINESS_EVENT_TIMESTAMP, MONETARY_TRIPLET, HEADER_REFERENCE) — concrete field names are inferred from the industry. Mandatory categories are the LAST things dropped at max-attribute caps. REFERENCE_LOOKUP and OTHER are exempt and must explain why via _canonical_skip_reason in the PK description. (v0.8.5 M5-FIX, alias=canonical-attrs-enforced)
Example: Every table has a role, and each role has a minimum set of details it must carry. An `order` acting as a transaction should have things like its own number, a status, a date, who it belongs to, and amounts, beyond just the identifier.

Name: Attribute Completeness Floor — Include ALL Business Fields
Requirement: Attribute generation MUST aim for comprehensive coverage: include EVERY business field the entity could have (identification, classification, status, amounts, dates, names, codes, descriptions, flags, measurements) and MUST NOT exclude a field merely because it might become an FK later (FKs added separately). Positive completeness floor, distinct from the min/max range check.
Example: Capture every business detail a table could reasonably have. For a `customer`, include name, contact, type, status, dates and codes; do not leave a field out just because it might later become a link.

Name: M:N Requires 3 Indicators
Requirement: M:N valid only when: (1) bidirectional reality, (2) >=2 relationship attributes, (3) business has name for relationship.
Example: Only create a connector table when the relationship is genuinely two-way, carries its own details, and has a real name. Students and courses linked by an `enrollment` that carries grades and dates qualifies.

Name: M:N Strong Indicators
Requirement: HIGH confidence requires >=2 of 3 strong indicators: reciprocity_confirmed, relationship_data_confirmed, semantic_name_found.
Example: Be confident before treating something as a many-to-many relationship. It needs at least two of three signals: both sides truly relate to many, the link carries its own data, and the business has a name for it.

Name: Association Ratio Limits
Requirement: ECM: max 15% association tables. MVM: max 5%. Hard-cap enforced.
Example: Limit how many tables are just connectors. In a 100-table model only about 15 should be connectors, and in a small model far fewer.

Name: MVM No Cross-Domain M:N
Requirement: Cross-domain M:N is FORBIDDEN in MVMs. Only in-domain M:N with >=3 relationship attributes.
Example: A small model should not have connector tables that span different areas. A within-area `enrollment` is fine, but cross-area connectors are not allowed in a small model.

Name: Core Products 1-3 Per Domain
Requirement: Select 1-3 CORE products per domain maximum. Core = fundamental to operations, cannot be merged, domain anchor.
Example: Pick only one to three core tables per area. In a sales area `customer`, `order` and `product` are core, while a `notification` table is not.

Name: Tiered Entity Selection
Requirement: Tier 1 (CORE-must include): master+transactional. Tier 2 (SUPPORTING-if first-class): operational+lifecycle. Tier 3 (REFERENCE-sparingly).
Example: Include the most essential tables first. Master and transaction tables like `customer` and `order` come first, supporting tables next, and reference tables only when they are rich enough to stand alone.

Name: Forbidden Products
Requirement: Forbidden: fraud_detection, churn_prediction, revenue_analysis, customer_360, unified_profile. Any *_analysis, *_analytics, *_prediction.
Example: Analytics-style tables do not belong in the operational model. A `churn_prediction` or `revenue_analysis` table belongs in the reporting layer, not here.

Name: Anti-Bloat Self-Check
Requirement: 5-point check: (1) Precision, (2) Domain Bleed, (3) Duplication, (4) Decomposition, (5) Coverage.
Example: Run a quick sanity check on each area's table list: is it precise, free of overlap and duplication, decomposed sensibly, and complete. Do this before finalizing.

Name: Small Table Handling
Requirement: Tables with fewer than min_attributes must be evaluated: MERGE, KEEP with justification, or DROP. A table is 'small' when it has fewer than the configured minimum attributes (default 5). Small tables must be evaluated: MERGE (columns belong on parent), KEEP (valid lookup/reference table), or DROP (exact semantic duplicate).
Example: A table with very few columns needs a decision: merge it, keep it, or drop it. A three-column `customer_phone` is probably just part of `customer` and should merge, while a `customer_type` lookup can be kept.

Name: Domain Boundary Discipline
Requirement: Vendors->partner. Contracts->agreement/legal. Employees->workforce/hr. Financial txns->finance. Customers->customer/party.
Example: Put tables in their natural home. An `employee` table belongs in the HR or workforce area, not in the production area.

Name: No FK in Attribute Step
Requirement: Do NOT include foreign key references during attribute generation. FKs established in separate linking step.
Example: Do not add links while listing a table's business columns. List all the real attributes first, then connect tables together in a later step.

Name: Silver Layer Only
Requirement: Attributes target Silver Layer: operational/transactional data only. No analytics, no Gold layer content.
Example: Keep only day-to-day operational fields. Include raw fields an `order` actually records, and leave calculated totals and scores to the reporting layer.

Name: MVM Domain Selection
Requirement: MVM must include: (1) Primary PARTY, (2) Primary TRANSACTIONAL, (3) Primary PRODUCT/SERVICE, (4) Essential OPERATIONAL.
Example: A small model must still cover the essentials: who the business serves, the main transaction, the product or service, and one key operational area.

Name: Mandatory Attributes by Type
Requirement: Person master -> name, contact, status. Account -> id, type, status, dates. Transaction -> id, date, status, amount.
Example: Each type of table has must-have fields. A `customer` master table needs a name, a contact method and a status; a transaction needs an identifier, date, status and amount.

Name: M:N Reject Analytical Correlations
Requirement: Analytical correlations derivable from transactional data are NOT valid M:N relationships.
Example: A pattern you can calculate from transactions is not a real relationship. A 'which customers buy which product categories' link is derived from order data, so it is not a true many-to-many.

Name: Comprehensive Party Coverage
Requirement: The model must provide comprehensive party/customer coverage (B2C, B2B, or mixed).
Example: Cover the full range of who the business deals with. A consumer business needs individual customer records, a business-to-business one needs company accounts, and a mixed one needs both.

Name: Validate Phantom Tables
Requirement: A new table should only be created for unlinked FKs when at least 2 different existing tables reference the same missing concept.
Example: Only invent a missing table when at least two existing tables point to it. If both `order` and `shipment` reference a missing `warehouse`, create it; a single lonely reference is probably just a stale link.

Name: Domain Product-Count Hard Ceiling
Requirement: No domain may hold more products than 15% above its sizing maximum. When a domain exceeds this ceiling, the excess products are removed in priority order (association first, then transactional, then reference, then master) so the most structurally load-bearing tables survive. An explicit user sizing directive overrides this ceiling.
Example: An area cannot hold far more tables than its target. If the target is 20 tables and an area swells past 23, the least important tables are trimmed first, unless the user asked for that size.

Name: M:N Granularity-Mismatch Rejection (Event vs Master = 1:N)
Requirement: A proposed M:N where one side is an EVENT/TRANSACTION entity (transaction, order_line, payment) and the other is a MASTER/REFERENCE entity (customer, product, store) MUST be auto-rejected as 1:N. Events touch many masters via an FK on the event, not a junction.
Example: An event linked to a master record is a one-to-many, not a many-to-many. An `order_line` touching many products does so through a simple link, not a connector table.

Name: M:N Reciprocity Confirmed in BOTH Directions
Requirement: An M:N may be accepted only when the LLM's `reciprocity_test` returns `a_to_many_b == true` AND `b_to_many_a == true`. Single-direction or unconfirmed reciprocity is auto-rejected (stronger than the "≥2 indicators" gate).
Example: A many-to-many is only accepted when both sides genuinely relate to many of the other. If only one direction holds, it is rejected and modelled as a simple link instead.

Name: M:N Justification Floor + Genuine Flag + Attr-Source Provenance
Requirement: An M:N candidate is rejected unless: `business_justification` ≥20 chars (ECM) / ≥40 chars (MVM); `is_genuine_m2m == true`; `naming_pattern != generic_link`; relationship-attr count ≥2 (ECM) / ≥3 (MVM). In MVM also requires `historical_tracking_needed == true` with a reason. Association non-FK attributes MUST originate only from detection `relationship_data`, attrs moved off A/B, or the two mandatory FKs — inventing attrs (enrollment_date, satisfaction_score) is forbidden.
Example: A connector table must earn its place: a real reason, its own attributes, a proper name, and genuine two-way meaning. Its extra columns must be real, not invented out of thin air.

Name: Industry Anchor Entities Mandatory Per Domain
Requirement: `industry_anchor_entities = {domain: [anchor_names]}` lists non-negotiable entities that MUST exist per domain for the industry (e.g. manufacturing production → production_order, work_center, bill_of_materials). All anchors with `must_have_for_scope ∈ {mvm, both}` must be present in MVM; all anchors must be present in ECM. Missing required anchors are a generation defect (optional ones → ANCHOR_OPTIONAL_MISSING).
Example: Each industry has must-have tables per area. A manufacturing production area should include things like a production order, work center and bill of materials; missing them is a gap.

Name: Regulatory-Reporting-Driven Entity Coverage
Requirement: `regulatory_reporting_requirements` (mandatory reports, each naming required data entities) MUST drive domain/product generation so all entities needed for each required report are modeled. `industry_compliance_frameworks` similarly require their regulatory domains/products in ECM.
Example: If the business must produce certain regulatory reports, the model must include every table those reports need. The required reports drive which tables and areas exist.

Name: Master-vs-Transaction Balance Per Domain
Requirement: Most operational domains need a mix of master and transactional records. A domain with only master records is likely missing operational activity; one with only transactions is likely missing the referenceable masters those transactions point to. The balance MUST be checked and gaps flagged.
Example: Most operational areas need a mix of reference tables and activity tables. An area with only master tables is missing the activity, and one with only transactions is missing the things they refer to.

Name: Duplicate Product-Pair Detection (X and prefixed_X)
Requirement: Within a single domain, the coexistence of a bare product X and a domain/concept-prefixed variant (goods_receipt AND procurement_goods_receipt) is an SSOT violation; the pair MUST be merged to one owner.
Example: Within one area, do not keep both a plain table and a prefixed version of the same thing. Holding both `goods_receipt` and `procurement_goods_receipt` is a duplicate; merge to one.

Name: Product Relocation Moves the Whole Cluster
Requirement: When a product is relocated to another domain, every product transitively related to it (its parent/child and tightly-coupled neighbours) must move together so a related cluster is never split across domains by a half-measure move.
Example: When you move a table, move its whole related cluster with it. Relocating `order` should also bring `order_line` and other children that only make sense alongside it.

Name: Association Tables Capped, Least-Critical Trimmed First
Requirement: When the share of association (junction) tables exceeds the cap (ECM 15%, MVM 5%), the least-critical associations must be removed first — ranked by low connectivity, low attribute richness, weak event semantics, and generic lazy names (_link/_map/_xref/_bridge) — until the model is within the cap.
Example: Keep connector tables under a cap and trim the weakest ones first. A thin `customer_product_link` with no real attributes is removed before a rich `enrollment` with grades and dates.

Name: No Dangling Orphan FK Columns
Requirement: An FK-shaped column (ending _id/_fk/_ref/_key) that cannot be resolved to any existing target entity must be removed, so the finished model contains no dangling orphan FK columns. A single unresolved reference must not spawn a speculative stub table.
Example: A link-shaped column that points to nothing must be removed. An `order.legacy_region_id` with no `region` table anywhere is dropped rather than spawning a made-up table.

Name: Master vs Transaction Balance Per Domain
Requirement: An operational domain should contain a mix of master/reference entities and transactional entities. A domain holding only masters is likely missing the operational activity that uses them; a domain holding only transactions is likely missing the referenceable masters those transactions point to.
Example: An operational area should mix reference tables and activity tables. A 'sales' area with only `customer` and `product` but no `order` is unbalanced and needs the transaction added.

Name: Industry Anchor Entities Present Per Domain
Requirement: Each domain must contain the non-negotiable anchor entities that define that business function for the industry. A domain missing its expected anchor entity is an incomplete model.
Example: Each area must contain the defining tables for that function in its industry. A manufacturing production area missing its production order or bill of materials is incomplete.

Name: Strict Column Range Limits
Requirement: The number of columns per table must fall within the configured minimum and maximum range.
Example: Each table should have a sensible number of columns. With a 10-to-25 range, a `customer` with only two columns is too thin, while one with 150 is an overstuffed table that should be split.

Name: Column Descriptions
Requirement: Every column must have a description explaining what business data it captures.
Example: Every column needs a description of what it captures. A bare `status` is unclear, while 'the current state of the claim: open, under review, approved or denied' is clear.

Name: Strict Domain Range Limits
Requirement: The number of domains must fall within the configured minimum and maximum range for the complexity tier.
Example: The model needs a sensible number of business areas. For a medium model, five to ten areas is right; two is too coarse and twenty-five is fragmented.

Name: No Tech Infrastructure Domains
Requirement: Domain names for technical infrastructure (logging, etl, integration, audit_trail, batch_control) are forbidden.
Example: Technical infrastructure names are not allowed as business areas. 'logging', 'etl', 'integration' and 'audit_trail' describe plumbing, not business functions.

Name: Distinct Domain Descriptions
Requirement: Every domain must have a description of at least 20 characters. No two domains may have >70% word overlap in descriptions.
Example: Each area needs a real description, and two areas should not have near-identical ones. 'finance' described as 'handles money' is too short, and 'billing' and 'finance' must not read almost the same.

Name: Minimum 3 Domains
Requirement: The model must contain at least 3 domains to be considered meaningful.
Example: A meaningful model has at least three business areas. A single 'general' area, or just 'customer' and 'product', is too thin and forces a better breakdown.

Name: Remove Empty Domains
Requirement: Domains that end up with zero products must be removed. User-defined required domains are protected.
Example: An area that ends up with no tables is removed, unless the user specifically required it. If 'logistics' ends up empty after cleanup, it is dropped.

Name: Strict Table Range Limits
Requirement: The number of tables per domain must fall within the configured minimum and maximum range.
Example: Each area needs a sensible number of tables. With a 5-to-10 range, an area with a single table is too narrow and one with thirty likely needs splitting.

Name: Table Descriptions
Requirement: Every table must have a description explaining its business purpose.
Example: Every table needs a description of its business purpose. A `subscription` table should explain that it tracks recurring agreements including plan, billing frequency and renewal terms.

Name: Metric Views Reference Only Columns on Their Own Source Table
Requirement: A metric view's dimensions and measures must reference only columns physically present on its single source product (no cross-table joins). A KPI needing data from another table must be re-sourced from a table that physically carries those columns, not expressed as a join.
Example: A report definition can only use columns that physically live on its one source table. A report built on `order` can use the order's own amount and status, but not the customer's region unless that lives on the order.

Name: Cross-Domain Connectivity
Requirement: Every domain MUST connect to at least one other domain via FK. Target: >=2 cross-domain connections per domain. A completely isolated domain with no cross-domain FKs is a data silo and a modeling error.
Example: Every area must connect to at least one other through links, ideally two. An isolated 'compliance' area with no connections to anything else is a silo and a modeling mistake.

Name: Lookup Tables Not Siloed
Requirement: Lookup tables that only have incoming FKs are NOT considered siloed. They are valid reference tables.
Example: A reference table that only receives links is not a silo. A `country` table with no outgoing links but many tables pointing to it is a perfectly valid lookup.

Name: FK Graph Is Acyclic (DAG)
Requirement: The foreign-key graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph: there must be no path A->B->...->A. Every FK relationship contributes a directed edge from the referencing product to the referenced product, and the resulting graph must contain no cycle.
Example: Links must never form a loop. You cannot have order pointing to invoice pointing back to order; if a loop forms, one link in it must be removed.

Name: Hierarchical Self-Reference Prefix List
Requirement: Self-referencing FKs are exempt from cycle/bidirectional detection ONLY when the FK column name starts with one of these recognized prefixes: parent_, manager_, reporting_, supervisor_, alternate_, original_, superseded_, duplicate_, follow_up_, ultimate_parent_, base_, amended_, reversal_, source_, target_, previous_, next_, replacement_, related_, primary_, secondary_, default_, upstream_, downstream_, child_, sibling_, ancestor_, successor_, predecessor_, preferred_, backup_, master_, derived_, copy_of_, from_, to_, old_, new_, current_, prior_, overflow_, escalation_, fallback_, redirect_, transfer_, forward_, return_, origin_.
Example: A table can point to itself only when the column name starts with a recognized relationship word. An `employee.manager_employee_id` pointing to `employee` is fine because of the 'manager' prefix; a plain `employee_id` self-link is not.

Name: Zero Siloed Tables
Requirement: A siloed table (no incoming AND no outgoing FKs) is STRICTLY PROHIBITED.
Example: A table with no links in and no links out is not allowed. A `lawful_intercept_request` table connected to nothing must be linked to at least one other table.

Name: Computed Reference Break First
Requirement: Computed/derived FK references broken FIRST in cycle resolution: latest_*, current_*, primary_*, active_*, default_*, first_*, last_*, preferred_*.
Example: When breaking a loop, cut calculated convenience links first. A `latest_invoice_id` is removed before a core `billing_account_id`, because it is just a shortcut.

Name: Minimize Cycle Breaks
Requirement: Many cycles share common edges. Breaking ONE edge can break 5-10+ cycles. Minimize unique breaks.
Example: Loops often share the same link, so cutting one well-chosen link can fix many at once. Look at all the loops together to find the shared link to break.

Name: Cycle Break Edge Verification
Requirement: Before breaking an edge, verify it actually exists in the cycle.
Example: Before cutting a link to break a loop, confirm that link is really part of the loop. Do not remove an edge that is not actually in the cycle.

Name: No Silo From Cycle Break
Requirement: A cycle break must NOT create a siloed table or siloed domain.
Example: Breaking a loop must not strand a table with no connections. If cutting one link would isolate a table, pick a different link to cut.

Name: Business Semantics Before Breaking
Requirement: Before breaking any cycle, analyze business semantics and cardinality. Child->Parent FK is always KEEP.
Example: Understand the business meaning before cutting any loop, and never cut a child-to-parent link. 'an invoice belongs to a billing account' means that direction stays.

Name: FK Anomaly Types
Requirement: Three FK anomaly types: (1) Missing Link, (2) Mismatched Link, (3) Cyclic Link.
Example: Link problems come in three kinds: a missing link, a link pointing at the wrong place, and a link that forms a loop. Each kind has its own fix.

Name: Residual FK Cycles Must Be Broken Deterministically
Requirement: If any FK cycle remains after semantic cycle resolution, the surviving cycle must be broken by removing the least-load-bearing edge in priority order (computed/derived reference first, then non-parent-child, then the edge shared by the most cycles). Parent-child and user-required FKs are never the edge removed.
Example: If a loop still remains after the smart cleanup, cut the least important link in it automatically, never a child-to-parent or user-required one. If three loops share one calculated link, removing that single link clears all three.

Name: No Cyclic FK Schema May Ship
Requirement: A finished model must contain zero FK cycles. A cyclic FK schema produces JOIN divergence and referential-integrity failures at query time, so any model with a surviving cycle is invalid and must not be emitted.
Example: A finished model must have zero loops. If `order` points to `invoice` and `invoice` points back to `order`, that loop is invalid and the model cannot ship.

Name: Attribute Belongs to Its Rightful Owner
Requirement: An attribute that describes a different entity than the product it currently sits on must be moved to the entity it truly describes, with an FK established back to it, rather than left as a denormalized copy.
Example: A column describing a different thing should move to that thing, with a link kept back. If `order` carries a 'customer loyalty tier' that really describes the customer, move it to `customer` and keep `order` linked by `customer_id`.

Name: PK Sequential
Requirement: BIGINT PKs must be sequential starting from 10001, NEVER NULL. STRING PKs must be valid UUIDs.
Example: Sample identifiers count up cleanly and are never blank. Numeric identifiers start at 10001 and increment: 10001, 10002, 10003, and so on.

Name: FK Random Range
Requirement: BIGINT FKs must be random values from [10001, 10001 + records - 1]. STRING FKs use UUIDs.
Example: Sample links pick a random valid identifier from the target table. For ten records, a link points at a random value between 10001 and 10010.

Name: PK/FK Exclusivity
Requirement: A column should NEVER be both a primary key AND a foreign key simultaneously.
Example: A column is either an identifier or a link in a given table, never both at once. `customer_id` is the identifier in `customer` but a link in `order`.

Name: Regex Compliance
Requirement: All values MUST comply with value_regex patterns defined on the attribute.
Example: Sample values must match the column's format rule. If a code field must be three uppercase letters, every sample value follows that exactly.

Name: Geographic Codes
Requirement: Country codes MUST be 3-letter uppercase ISO format. No regional names (EU, LATAM).
Example: Sample country values use the three-letter uppercase code. Use 'USA', 'GBR' or 'DEU', not 'United States' or a region like 'EMEA'.

Name: Exact Record Count
Requirement: Generate EXACTLY the configured number of records per table. No more, no fewer.
Example: Generate exactly the requested number of sample rows. If ten rows are configured, every table gets exactly ten, no more and no fewer.

Name: No Lorem Ipsum
Requirement: Data MUST be realistic and business-appropriate. NO Lorem Ipsum or placeholder text.
Example: Sample data should look realistic, not like filler. Use believable names, addresses and amounts, never 'John Doe', 'Test Company' or placeholder text.

Name: Attribute Dedup Confidence
Requirement: Only flag attribute duplicates when >80% confident they represent the SAME business concept. False positives worse than false negatives.
Example: Only merge two columns when you are quite sure they mean the same thing. 'creation_date' and 'created_at' are clearly the same and can merge, but 'start_date' and 'end_date' are different and stay.

Name: No Name Invention in Merge
Requirement: When merging product attributes, NEVER introduce new attribute names - only choose among existing attributes.
Example: When merging columns, pick from the existing names rather than inventing a new one. Choose the better of the two real names; do not make up a third.

Name: High-Confidence Column Dedup
Requirement: When checking for duplicate columns within a table, only flag them with 80% or higher confidence.
Example: Only flag two columns in a table as duplicates when you are highly confident. 'termination_date' and 'end_date' at high confidence can merge, but a weak 60% guess does not.

Name: Protect Key Attributes
Requirement: PK and FK attributes are protected from removal during attribute deduplication. They must never be flagged as duplicates.
Example: Identifier and linking columns are protected from being merged away. If `customer_id` and a `client_id` business field look alike, only the business field can be considered, never the identifier.

Name: Unique Domain Names
Requirement: No two domains may have the same name.
Example: Two business areas cannot share a name. If one finance area handles accounting and another handles investment, name them 'accounting' and 'investment' instead of both 'finance'.

Name: First-Class Entity Test
